blocks.text: I can use verbs with prepositions, in the context of a school exchange.
You will also learn to pronounce [-ig] correctly.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word.
A verb followed by a preposition which links it to a noun.

blocks.text: At the end of a word, [-ig] sounds like a soft [ch], as in ‘ich’. In Austria, it sounds like ‘k’!
Tap a word to see what it means.

slides.title: When [ig] is followed by a vowel

blocks.text: When [ig] is followed by a vowel, the g becomes vocal, making a hard sound, like in ‘egg’.

blocks.label: What do you notice?
blocks.text: In ‘richtig’ the g is a soft sound, as in ‘ich’. In ‘richtige’ the g changes to a hard g, as in ‘egg’.

blocks.q: In which word is the g a hard sound, like in ‘egg’?
blocks.why: In ‘wichtiges’ the g is followed by a vowel (e), so it is a hard g. In ‘wichtig’ and ‘lustig’ it is at the end of the word, so it is a soft [ch] sound.

blocks.text: Sometimes verbs are followed by prepositions which link them to a noun. We call them prepositional verbs.

items: Meine Freunde warnen mich vor dem Wetter. (My friends are warning me about the weather.)
Ich interessiere mich für dieses Schulfach. (I’m interested in this school subject.)

blocks.text: Prepositions used with some verbs in German may not be the same as those used with the same verbs in English.

slides.title: Learn the verb with its preposition

blocks.text: We often use different prepositions after verbs in English and German, so the verb and preposition combinations need to be learnt. Tap each one.

blocks.label: What do you notice?
blocks.text: ‘To hope for’ and ‘to wait for’ both use ‘for’ in English, and both use auf in German. But ‘to take part in’ uses an in German, not ‘in’.

blocks.q: Match the German to the English.

blocks.text: Prepositions may change the form of the article that follows, as they are used with specific cases.

items: Ich interessiere mich für dieses Schulfach. (accusative)
Meine Freunde warnen mich vor dem Wetter. (dative)

slides.title: Auf and an: learn each verb

items: Verbs with {auf} are often followed by the accusative: Alastair freut sich auf unseren Besuch.
Verbs with {an} are often followed by the dative: Meine Freunde nehmen an einem Austausch teil.

blocks.text: We must learn which case is used with an or auf when we learn each verb.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: Vor, like an and auf, can be used with the accusative sometimes, but after prepositional verbs vor always takes the dative.

blocks.q: Choose the preposition that goes with the verb.
Choose the correct article. Check the case the preposition needs.
Is the noun phrase after the preposition in the accusative or the dative?

items.text: Ich freue mich auf den Austausch.
Wir haben ein Geschenk für die Familie.
Ich habe Angst vor der Party.
Die Lehrerin hofft auf ein schönes Wochenende.

blocks.q: Match the start of each question to its ending.

blocks.text: Wolfgang writes to Alastair: ‘Ich hoffe trotzdem auf gutes Wetter für den Austausch!’

blocks.q: Which is the best English translation of ‘Wolfgang hofft trotzdem auf gutes Wetter’?
options: Wolfgang nevertheless hopes for good weather.
Wolfgang nevertheless hopes on good weather.
Wolfgang is afraid of good weather.
blocks.why: ‘Hoffen auf’ means ‘to hope for’. German uses auf where English uses ‘for’.

items: At the end of a word, [-ig] is a soft [ch], as in ‘richtig’. In Austria, it sounds like [k].
Prepositions used with some verbs in German may not be the same as in English.
Prepositions may change the form of the article that follows, because they are used with specific cases.
Verbs with ‘für’ are always followed by the accusative; verbs with ‘vor’ by the dative.
Verbs with ‘auf’ usually take the accusative; verbs with ‘an’ are often followed by the dative.

flashcards.front: How is [-ig] pronounced at the end of a word, as in ‘richtig’?
flashcards.back: As a soft [ch], as in ‘ich’. (In Austria it sounds like [k].)

flashcards.front: What happens to the g in ‘richtig’ when a vowel follows, as in ‘richtige’?
flashcards.back: The g becomes vocal and hard, like in ‘egg’.
A word used before a noun, a noun phrase or a pronoun, connecting it to another word.

flashcards.front: Do German and English always use the same preposition with a verb?
flashcards.back: No. Prepositions used with some verbs in German may not be the same as in English. Learn each verb with its preposition.

flashcards.front: Which case do verbs with ‘für’ always take?
flashcards.back:
The accusative.

Ich interessiere mich für dieses Schulfach.

flashcards.front: Which case do verbs with ‘vor’ always take?
flashcards.back:
The dative.

Meine Freunde warnen mich vor dem Wetter.

flashcards.front: Which case do verbs with ‘auf’ usually take?
flashcards.back:
The accusative.

Alastair freut sich auf unseren Besuch.

flashcards.front: Which case are verbs with ‘an’ often followed by?
flashcards.back:
The dative.

Meine Freunde nehmen an einem Austausch teil.

flashcards.front: Say in German: ‘to take part in’
Say in German: ‘to look forward to’
Say in German: ‘to be afraid of’
Say in German: ‘to be interested in’
What do ‘hoffen auf’ and ‘warten auf’ mean?
flashcards.back: hoffen auf = to hope for; warten auf = to wait for. Both use auf.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: A school exchange: verbs with prepositions ‘an’, ‘auf’, ‘für’, ‘vor’
worksheet.instructions: Fill the gap with one word, or answer the question. Use what you learnt about verbs with prepositions.

questions.prompt: Task B: Hast du Angst ___ dem Monster? Write the missing preposition.
questions.explanation: ‘Angst haben vor’ means ‘to be afraid of’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Nimmst du ___ der Aktivität teil? Write the missing preposition.
Task B: Interessierst du dich ___ Geschichte? Write the missing preposition.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich interessieren für’ means ‘to be interested in’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Freust du dich ___ die Party? Write the missing preposition.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich freuen auf’ means ‘to look forward to’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Ich habe Angst vor ___ Party. Write the correct definite article (‘Party’ is feminine and must be in the dative here).
questions.explanation: ‘Vor’ takes the dative, and the feminine dative article is ‘der’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Wir haben ein Geschenk für ___ Familie. Write the correct definite article.
questions.explanation: ‘Für’ always takes the accusative, and the feminine accusative article is ‘die’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Ich freue mich schon auf ___ nächsten Austausch. Write the correct definite article.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich freuen auf’ takes the accusative, and the masculine accusative article is ‘den’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Alastair interessiert sich für ___ Wandern. Write the correct definite article.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich interessieren für’ takes the accusative, and ‘das Wandern’ stays ‘das’.

questions.prompt: Which case do verbs with the preposition ‘für’ always take?
questions.explanation: Verbs with ‘für’ are always followed by the accusative.

questions.prompt: Which case do verbs with the preposition ‘vor’ always take?
questions.explanation: Verbs with ‘vor’ are always followed by the dative.

questions.prompt: Give the English for ‘sich freuen auf’.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich freuen auf’ means ‘to look forward to’.
